title: Whither thou goest (Ruth 1)
hookLine: a Moabite widow refuses to leave her mother-in-law: thy people shall be my people

cards: Three widows stand on a road. One is old: Naomi, Noemi in the Douay-Rheims. She left Bethlehem in a famine with her husband and two sons, and in the land of Moab she lost all three.
The other two are young Moabite women who married her sons. Now Naomi is walking home with nothing, and she tells them: go back to your mothers. I have no more sons for you.
They cry. One of them, Orpah, kisses her and turns back, and nobody in the story blames her. The other one won't let go.

teach.h: WHITHER THOU GOEST, I WILL GO.
teach.b: What Ruth says next has traveled far beyond this book. In older English it's remembered as whither thou goest, I will go.
The Douay-Rheims gives it like this: "whithersoever thou shalt go, I will go: and where thou shalt dwell, I also will dwell. Thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God."
She goes further: where you die, I'll die, and there I'll be buried. Notice who she's saying it to. Not a husband.

A mother-in-law, old, grieving and broke, who has just told her to leave. Some couples choose these words for their weddings, but first they were a daughter-in-law's vow to a widow with nothing to offer.
The Hebrew storytellers have a word for what Ruth does: chesed, steady, loyal love that keeps showing up.
Naomi even uses it on the road, praying that God will deal kindly with the two young women, as they have dealt with the dead and with her.
Ruth is a foreigner, from Moab, a people Israel had old quarrels with, and she becomes, in this book, the picture of faithfulness. In Bethlehem the town women say, is this Naomi?
And Naomi answers, in the Douay: "I went out full, and the Lord hath brought me back empty." Don't call me Naomi, she says, which means beautiful.

teach.h: THY PEOPLE SHALL BE MY PEOPLE.
teach.b: The book lets her say it. It doesn't correct her or rush her. It just keeps Ruth standing beside her, through the bitterness, at the start of the barley harvest.

how: Catholics hear Ruth's story in the weekday Mass readings, and hear her name again in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus, where she stands among his ancestors.

steady, loyal love that keeps showing up

s: Ruth first spoke these words to a husband
she said them to Naomi, her widowed mother-in-law, on the road to Bethlehem.
Ruth was a Moabite, not an Israelite
a foreigner, and the book makes her the picture of loyal love.
the story blames Orpah for going home
Naomi told both to go back. Orpah obeys, kisses her and leaves, and the text doesn't condemn her.

games.q: you're Ruth. your husband is dead, your mother-in-law is going back to a country you've never seen, and she's told you to go home. what do you do?
o: kiss her goodbye and go home, like Orpah.
promise to go where she goes, live where she lives, and be buried where she's buried.
go with her as far as the border.
games.why: Ruth won't leave: thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God. a vow of loyal love made to a widow with nothing to give back.

practice: Think of someone who is grieving right now, a death, a divorce, a diagnosis, a move they didn't want, maybe someone who, like Naomi, has told everyone to go away.
Picture yourself on the road beside them, not fixing anything, just walking. If you pray, hold them before God by name; if not, simply stay beside them in your mind a while.

wordCard.voice: chesed. Hebrew for steady, loyal love that keeps showing up, the word for Ruth's promise to Naomi, a widow who had nothing left. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: loyal, steadfast love. Naomi uses it on the road, and it runs through the whole Book of Ruth.

carryVoice: Your line: thy people, my people. Loyal love doesn't wait to be asked. See you tomorrow.
